title: Record your AI avatar once: an open-source AI HR hunter (and why it never presses Send on LinkedIn)
author: Evgenii Arsentev
summary: I wrote hireburn and put it under MIT. It's a Python CLI, standard library only, with no network calls, so nothing leaves your machine. Why the avatar part exists People put off recording an avatar because they picture a studio. You need a window, a phone and twenty minutes, once. After that the avatar asks every candidate the same questions in the same words, so the first interviews can be compared with each other. The candidate page says they are talking to an AI avatar before they press Start. The scoring rubric always puts a warning next to the HIRE / MAYBE / NO label: the label is not a measurement. The part where it does not press Send hireburn drafts LinkedIn outreach and reminders from a template plus a hook line that a person writes after reading the profile. The queue has random pauses, hourly and daily limits, and working hours. It has a STOP button for the first warning or captcha, and a reply tracker. A human presses Send. hireburn never does. We got a LinkedIn restriction when our pace was not human. Bots in this area get their accounts limited, and that's why the default limits are what they are. Where the funnel leaks The funnel leaks where nobody looks. No-shows, bookings nobody updated, people who got access and never started, decisions that sat for weeks. hireburn shows the loss at each stage and the days until first real work. It also puts the AI label next to whether that person is still working on day N. In the case this method grew out of, the AI interview labels did not match who was still working weeks later. So the tool puts the label beside the outcome, and you can check it on your own people. Try it The demo runs on a synthetic company, and all its numbers are invented and round on purpose. pip install hireburn hireburn demo Telling the candidate is a feature here. Disclosure, consent, a human alternative and human review are built into the page and the rubric, so the lawful path is the default one. There is also a disclosure checklist for NYC Local Law 144, the Illinois AI Video Interview Act, Illinois HB 3773 and the EU AI Act (hiring is high-risk under Annex III). It's a guide, not legal advice. This is part of the payrollburn series of cases about AI managers in a live company. The method report is at doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23927437 , and the story of the case is on DEV.to: AI hiring in a live company . title: Before You Save an LLM Response to Your Database
author: Alex Agafonov
summary: Consider a small service that extracts an invoice line: item code, quantity, unit price, and total. The response arrives as JSON, and Pydantic creates an object without an error. It is tempting to pass that object straight to the write step and call the job finished. Look at the numbers. The quantity is three, the unit price is 2500, and the line total is also 2500. Every value is a positive integer. But three units at 2500 should give 7500. The line needs a closer look before we save it. For this case, I would separate the work into three steps: parse the response, check the rules of the task, and prepare a result for the next stage. A small Python function will show the boundary. It returns a draft or a reason for human review, without calling a model or a database. What we asked Pydantic to check Start with the schema. Prices and totals in this example use the minor units of a single currency. Taxes, discounts, and rounding are outside this simplified calculation. from pydantic import BaseModel , ConfigDict , Field , ValidationError class ExtractedLine ( BaseModel ): model_config = ConfigDict ( strict = True , extra = " forbid " , frozen = True ) sku : str = Field ( min_length = 1 ) quantity : int = Field ( gt = 0 ) unit_price_minor : int = Field ( ge = 0 ) line_total_minor : int = Field ( ge = 0 ) We have described the fields and constraints: a nonempty item code, a positive quantity, and nonnegative prices and totals. Extra fields are forbidden. In this example, strict mode prevents the string "3" from being quietly converted to an integer. The strict mode documentation explains that behavior. Now pass an object with the wrong total: payload = { " sku " : " KB-01 " , " quantity " : 3 , " unit_price_minor " : 2500 , " line_total_minor " : 2500 , } line = ExtractedLine . model_validate ( payload ) print ( line . quantity , line . line_total_minor ) The output is: 3 2500 Pydantic performed the checks we specified. The schema contained no rule connecting quantity, price, and total. The guarantee described in the model documentation also concerns the declared types and constraints. We still have to express the rule for our task. The order comes from the application We need context as well as arithmetic. Does the item belong to the selected order? Does the price match? Does the quantity exceed the amount still outstanding? For this example, assume the application has already selected an order and loaded its trusted line. A price difference, an unknown item, or a quantity above the remaining amount goes to review. These are the rules of our teaching example, rather than universal rules for processing invoices. The model does not choose the order ID or its revision. The application obtains them from its own system. Words in the document or a field in the JSON must not switch processing to a different order. A small check of the task's rules Add the following classes and functions to the ExtractedLine definition. Together, they form invoice_validation.py : from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class OrderLine : order_id : str revision : int sku : str unit_price_minor : int remaining_quantity : int @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class DraftLine : order_id : str order_revision : int sku : str quantity : int line_total_minor : int @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class NeedsReview : reason : str def check_line ( line : ExtractedLine , order : OrderLine ) -> DraftLine | NeedsReview : if line . sku != order . sku : return NeedsReview ( " unknown_item " ) if line . quantity > order . remaining_quantity : return NeedsReview ( " quantity_exceeds_order " ) if line . unit_price_minor != order . unit_price_minor : return NeedsReview ( " price_differs " ) expected_total = line . quantity * order . unit_price_minor if line . line_total_minor != expected_total : return NeedsReview ( " total_mismatch " ) return DraftLine ( order_id = order . order_id , order_revision = order . revision , sku = order . sku , quantity = line . quantity , line_total_minor = expected_total , ) def prepare_line ( payload : dict [ str , object ], order : OrderLine ) -> DraftLine | NeedsReview : try : line = ExtractedLine . model_validate ( payload ) except ValidationError : return NeedsReview ( " invalid_shape " ) return check_line ( line , order ) prepare_line receives an already decoded JSON object. Obtaining the response and handling JSON syntax errors sit outside this function. It checks the shape first, then passes the object to check_line , where the rules for the selected order are visible. OrderLine is trusted application context. This function does not check how it was loaded or who authorized access to the order. It must not be built from the same model response we are trying to validate. Notice what happens to the inconsistent total. The function does not silently replace it with 7500. It returns total_mismatch , because the mistake could be in the quantity, price, or total. Multiplication alone cannot tell us which field to change. See the difference without calling a model Use an order with a unit price of 2500 and five units outstanding: order = OrderLine ( " PO-17 " , 4 , " KB-01 " , 2500 , 5 ) print ( prepare_line ( payload , order )) corrected = { ** payload , " line_total_minor " : 7500 } print ( prepare_line ( corrected , order )) The result is: NeedsReview(reason='total_mismatch') DraftLine(order_id='PO-17', order_revision=4, sku='KB-01', quantity=3, line_total_minor=7500) We changed the second object manually to check an allowed case. It is not another response from a real model, and it tells us nothing about extraction quality. Alongside that case, I would test a string in place of the quantity, an unknown item, an excessive quantity, and a different price. Extra order_id or order_revision fields should also be rejected: the application has already selected that context. These checks need neither a live database nor an external API. The accompanying example has eight tests covering an allowed result, review reasons, and unchanged inputs. The code was checked with Python 3.12.14 and Pydantic 2.14.1. Arithmetic does not verify the document Now take a more troublesome case. The original invoice says three units, but the model returns two and correctly multiplies the price by two: plausible = { ** payload , " quantity " : 2 , " line_total_minor " : 5000 } result = prepare_line ( plausible , order ) assert result == DraftLine ( " PO-17 " , 4 , " KB-01 " , 2 , 5000 ) This result passes our checks. The item is known, the quantity fits within the outstanding amount, the price matches, and the arithmetic is correct. The quantity still disagrees with the original invoice. That boundary needs to stay visible. We checked the fields against the specified rules; comparison with the original still needs a place in the process. I would show the specialist the source document alongside the proposed values. Ambiguous or contradictory extraction calls for clarification or manual review. Filling a missing required field with zero just to complete processing would hide the problem. Some comparisons may be automated against a reliable source. Another call to the same model, however, does not by itself make the check independent or establish that the numbers are right. The two-instead-of-three case is included in the tests specifically to show this limit. These rules can also live inside Pydantic Pydantic supports field and model validators . For example, a model_validator could check that the total equals quantity multiplied by price. I used a separate function here so that the order context and the decision are visible together: a draft or a reason for review. If a team finds it clearer to express some conditions inside Pydantic, that is a reasonable choice. What matters is which rules actually run and which information they rely on. Receiving a DraftLine does not finish the job either. Before an actual write, the application must check permissions, the current order state, and acceptance conditions. Keeping the order revision can help detect a change, but it does not lock the order or replace a check at write time. Transactions, repeated invoice processing, and the specialist's final decision need their own process; this function does not implement them. I want the calling code to understand the result precisely: the fields were parsed, the listed rules passed, and a draft was prepared for the selected order. If we later discover that the model misread the quantity, we can identify the comparison we have yet to arrange. A successful model_validate call should leave that question visible. References Pydantic. Models . Pydantic. Strict Mode . Pydantic. Validators .

summary: ज़्यादातर YouTube वीडियो में ट्रांसक्रिप्ट होती है, और उनमें से अधिकतर को स्पीच रिकग्निशन ने लिखा होता है। वीडियो के साथ चलने के लिए यह ठीक है। लेकिन किसी पेपर, न्यूज़ स्टोरी या क़ानूनी नोट में कोट देने के लिए सवाल यह है कि ऑटोमैटिक टेक्स्ट असल में कही गई बात से कितना दूर है, और उसके टाइमस्टैम्प सही सेकंड पर इशारा करते हैं या नहीं। जिस वीडियो में दोनों तरह के कैप्शन हों, वह इसका सीधा जवाब देता है। वीडियो NASA का अपलोड किया हुआ राष्ट्रपति कैनेडी का 1962 का राइस यूनिवर्सिटी वाला भाषण है ( WZyRbnpGyzQ , 18 मिनट)। इसमें दो अंग्रेज़ी ट्रैक हैं: एक किसी इंसान का लिखा हुआ और एक YouTube का बनाया हुआ। दोनों को Python पैकेज youtube-transcript-api से लिस्ट और डाउनलोड किया जा सकता है: from youtube_transcript_api import YouTubeTranscriptApi tracks = YouTubeTranscriptApi (). list ( " WZyRbnpGyzQ " ) for t in tracks : print ( t . language_code , t . is_generated , t . language ) # en False English - सायटेशन के तौर पर दोनों ग़लत हैं। इस मामले में व्याकरण बचा रहा, "they are", उस वर्शन के उलट जो ज़्यादातर लोगों को याद है ("because it is hard")। लेकिन कुछ लाइनों बाद "we are willing" बन गया "we're willing", और ऑटोमैटिक ट्रैक से लिया गया कोट कैनेडी के मुँह में ऐसा संक्षिप्त रूप डाल देगा जो उन्होंने कहा ही नहीं। ट्रैक चुनना, और लिंक osFoundry डेस्कटॉप ऐप का ट्रांसक्रिप्ट टूल, जो उसी कंप्यूटर से कैप्शन लाता है जिस पर वह चल रहा है, यह चुनाव Rust की कुछ लाइनों में करता है। YouTube ऑटोमैटिक ट्रैक को kind: "asr" से चिह्नित करता है, और ऐप पहले इंसान का लिखा अंग्रेज़ी ट्रैक लेता है, फिर कोई भी अंग्रेज़ी ट्रैक, फिर कोई भी इंसानी ट्रैक, और फिर जो भी मौजूद हो: fn pick_track ( tracks : & [ CaptionTrack ]) -> Option <& CaptionTrack > { tracks .iter () .find (| t | t .language_code .starts_with ( "en" ) && t .kind != "asr" ) .or_else (|| tracks .iter () .find (| t | t .language_code .starts_with ( "en" ))) .or_else (|| tracks .iter () .find (| t | t .kind != "asr" )) .or_else (|| tracks .first ()) } जब कोई लाइन रेफ़रेंस के रूप में सेव होती है, तो उसका स्टार्ट टाइम लिंक का t पैरामीटर बन जाता है। समय नीचे की ओर राउंड किया जाता है, ताकि वीडियो शब्दों से सेकंड के एक हिस्से पहले शुरू हो, पहले शब्द के बाद नहीं: url : `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v= ${ transcript . video_id } &t= ${ Math . floor ( segment . start )} s` 9:18 वाली लाइन के लिए यह &t=558s है, उस लाइन के लिए जो 558.9 सेकंड पर शुरू होती है। जब सिर्फ़ ऑटोमैटिक ट्रैक हो बहुत से वीडियो में सिर्फ़ ऑटोमैटिक ट्रैक होता है। तब वह सर्च इंडेक्स है, स्रोत नहीं: उससे मोटे तौर पर पता करें कि बात कहाँ कही गई, वह हिस्सा चलाएँ और कोट ऑडियो सुनकर लिखें। नाम और संख्याएँ किसी दूसरे स्रोत से जाँचें, और ऐसे हिस्सों की उम्मीद रखें जो बिना किसी निशान के ग़ायब हैं। सेकंड तक पहुँचने वाला लिंक फिर भी रखने लायक़ है, क्योंकि उससे पाठक वही जाँच कुछ सेकंड में दोहरा सकता है। यहाँ इस्तेमाल हुआ डेस्कटॉप ऐप osFoundry डाउनलोड पेज से मुफ़्त है।

title: Por qué du y el Finder muestran tamaños distintos para la misma carpeta
author: Hanako H.
summary: Ejecuta du -sh sobre una carpeta y compáralo con el tamaño del Finder: a menudo no coinciden, a veces por varios gigabytes. Ninguno se equivoca. Responden a preguntas distintas: cuánto miden los archivos y cuánto espacio del disco ocupan. Cuando el disco está lleno solo importa la segunda, y calcularla bien exige algo más que sumar st_size . Las reglas de abajo son las que sigue la pantalla Disk de la aplicación de escritorio osFoundry . Su escáner es una función corta de Rust sobre std::fs , y la misma lógica cabe en unas 40 líneas de Python. Todos los números salen de una carpeta de prueba en un volumen APFS con bloques de asignación de 4 KB. Cuenta bloques, no bytes st_size es la longitud del archivo. st_blocks es el número de unidades de 512 bytes que el sistema de archivos ha asignado, sea cual sea el tamaño de bloque real del volumen. El escáner de la aplicación usa por defecto la segunda: fn allocated_bytes ( meta : & fs :: Metadata , apparent : bool ) -> u64 { if apparent { return meta .len (); } #[cfg(unix)] { use std :: os :: unix :: fs :: MetadataExt ; meta .blocks () .saturating_mul ( 512 ) } #[cfg(not(unix))] { meta .len () } } Tres archivos de la carpeta de prueba muestran por qué: Archivo st_size st_blocks × 512 small.txt (2 bytes de texto) 2 4,096 sparse.img (truncado a 1 GiB, nunca escrito) 1,073,741,824 0 big.bin (200 MiB de datos) 209,715,200 209,715,200 Un archivo diminuto ocupa igualmente un bloque entero, así que una carpeta con 100.000 archivos pequeños ocupa en disco varios cientos de megabytes más de lo que indica su recuento de bytes. Un archivo disperso (sparse) es lo contrario: los discos de máquinas virtuales, los archivos de bases de datos y algunas descargas reservan una longitud grande y solo usan bloques en las partes escritas. El du de macOS cuenta bloques; du -A muestra el tamaño aparente. La casilla Apparent size de la aplicación hace ese mismo cambio. No sigas enlaces ni salgas del volumen Un escáner que sigue enlaces simbólicos puede contar dos veces la misma carpeta, o entrar en un bucle infinito con un enlace que apunta a su propio directorio padre. Uno que entra en una unidad montada suma los archivos de otro disco al total de este. La aplicación lee cada entrada con symlink_metadata , que describe el enlace y no su destino, y compara los ID de dispositivo con los de la carpeta donde empezó el escaneo: if child_meta .file_type () .is_symlink () || ! same_device ( root_meta , & child_meta ) { continue ; } same_device compara st_dev , que es la misma comprobación que hacen du -x o find -xdev . Enlaces duros y clones Los enlaces duros son un único archivo con varios nombres. En la carpeta de prueba, ln big.bin hard.bin hace que ls -l muestre dos archivos de 200 MiB, pero du cuenta los datos una sola vez porque recuerda cada par (st_dev, st_ino) que ya ha visto siempre que st_nlink sea mayor que 1. Cualquier escáner que sume bloques debería hacer lo mismo. Las copias de Time Machine en discos HFS+ y algunos gestores de paquetes dependen mucho de los enlaces duros. Los clones de APFS son más difíciles. cp -c big.bin clone.bin (o Duplicar en el Finder) crea un segundo archivo que comparte los bloques del original hasta que uno de los dos cambia. Cada archivo tiene su propio inodo, su propio st_blocks y un recuento de enlaces de 1, de modo que du cuenta 400 MiB para el par. Medido con df antes y después, el clon ocupó 0 KB de espacio libre, mientras que un cp normal del mismo archivo ocupó 204.984 KB. Ningún campo POSIX muestra que se comparten bloques, así que un total basado en bloques exagera lo que se recupera al borrar un clon. Para carpetas llenas de proyectos duplicados o bibliotecas de fotos, comparar df antes y después es la única comprobación fiable. Una versión en Python Las mismas reglas, solo con la biblioteca estándar: import os import stat import sys def usage ( root ): root_dev = os . lstat ( root ). st_dev seen = set () allocated = apparent = 0 skipped = 0 stack = [ root ] while stack : path = stack . pop () try : entries = list ( os . scandir ( path )) except OSError : skipped += 1 continue for e in entries : try : st = e . stat ( follow_symlinks = False ) except OSError : skipped += 1 continue if stat . S_ISLNK ( st . st_mode ) or st . st_dev != root_dev : continue if stat . S_ISDIR ( st . st_mode ): stack . append ( e . path ) continue if st . st_nlink > 1 : key = ( st . st_dev , st . st_ino ) if key in seen : continue seen . add ( key ) allocated += st . st_blocks * 512 apparent += st . st_size return allocated , apparent , skipped if __name__ == " __main__ " : alloc , appar , skipped = usage ( sys . argv [ 1 ]) print ( f " on disk { alloc / 2 ** 30 : 8.2 f } GiB " ) print ( f " apparent { appar / 2 ** 30 : 8.2 f } GiB " ) if skipped : print ( f " skipped { skipped } unreadable entries " ) En la carpeta de prueba imprime 0,39 GiB en disco y 1,39 GiB aparentes, lo que coincide con du -sk (409.604 KB) y du -sAk . En un árbol de código fuente de 14 GiB coincide con du -sk hasta dos decimales. Conserva el recuento de entradas omitidas: en macOS, las carpetas protegidas por permisos de privacidad (Mail, Mensajes, Safari) no se pueden leer sin Acceso total al disco, y un total que las deja fuera sin avisar parece más completo de lo que es. La aplicación mantiene el resultado lo bastante pequeño como para dibujarlo. Cada carpeta conserva sus 36 hijos más grandes y el resto se suma en un único nodo "Other items"; así, al abrir una carpeta node_modules con mil paquetes se ven 36 cajas y una más para todo lo demás, no mil rendijas. Borrar con seguridad El verdadero riesgo de una herramienta de disco está en el paso de borrar. La aplicación mueve los elementos a la Papelera del sistema con el crate trash en lugar de eliminarlos con unlink, y comprueba cada ruta antes de mover nada: if ! target .starts_with ( & root ) || target == root || home .as_ref () == Some ( & target ) { return Err ( "Cannot move a scan root or home folder to Trash" .into ()); } if mount_points .iter () .any (| mount | target == * mount || target .parent () == Some ( mount .as_path ())) { return Err ( "Cannot move a volume or its top-level items to Trash" .into ()); } Las rutas se canonicalizan primero, de modo que .. o un enlace simbólico no pueden colar un destino fuera de la carpeta escaneada. También se rechaza una selección en la que una carpeta marcada contiene a otra, porque en cuanto la carpeta padre está en la Papelera la ruta del hijo deja de existir y el lote fallaría a medias. La aplicación de escritorio es gratuita en la página de descarga de osFoundry .

title: Search Intent Explained: Why Great Content Still Fails to Rank
author: fana
summary: You spent hours on a post. It's well written, well researched, even nicely formatted. And it sits on page six of Google, doing nothing. If that's happened to you, az s a freelance digital marketing expert in Thrissur I can tell you the most likely culprit isn't quality. It's search intent. What search intent actually means Search intent is the reason behind a search. Someone typing a phrase into Google wants something specific, and Google tries to show whatever satisfies that want best. If your page gives a different kind of answer than what people are looking for, it won't rank, however good it is. The four common types Informational: "how to start a blog," "what is a backlink." The person wants to learn something. Navigational: "Facebook login," "Google Search Console." The person wants to reach a specific site. Commercial: "best SEO tools," "WordPress vs Wix." The person is comparing options before deciding. Transactional: "buy running shoes online," "hire SEO freelancer." The person is ready to act. A quick example of getting it wrong Say you write a long guide called "Everything About Email Marketing" and aim it at the phrase "email marketing software." But people searching that phrase want to compare tools and pick one. If your page is a general beginner's guide, you're answering a question they didn't ask. Now flip it. A beautiful product comparison page won't rank for "what is email marketing," because that searcher wants an explanation, not a buying guide. How to check intent in two minutes Search your target keyword in Google. Look at the top five results. Are they guides, lists, product pages or videos? Notice the format and the angle. Are they "how-to" posts? Comparisons? Short definitions? Ask yourself what the searcher would need to see to feel finished. Google's top results are basically a hint sheet telling you what people want. Fixing a post that isn't ranking Match the format. If the top results are listicles, a long essay may struggle. Match the stage. Don't push a sales pitch on someone who's still learning. Answer the main question fast. Don't make people hunt for it. Cover related questions. Look at the "People also ask" box for ideas on what else to include. Update the title and intro so they clearly reflect what the page delivers. Don't force one page to do everything Sometimes the right move is to split content. One page for beginners, another for comparison, another for buyers. Each can target a different intent and a different phrase. The short version Before you write, ask: "What does this person want when they type this?" Then build the page around that answer. Great content that matches intent will beat great content that ignores it, every single time.

title: Scoring browser games on the server so players can't cheat
author: dziulatex
summary: I build GamePrep, a free practice site for the "games" employers use in hiring: HireVue, Arctic Shores, Aon, Wonderlic-style tests. 39 browser games, each one ends with a score and a percentile. Two lessons from building it, one about trust and one about norms: Never let the browser decide the score. Not because people cheat on a free practice site, but because the moment the score lives in JavaScript, it means nothing. Simulated norms are a guess. Mine were wrong by a mile, and real players told me so. The stack is Laravel + vanilla JS, but the pattern works anywhere. The contract: the browser sends what happened, the server decides what it means Every game is a PHP class plus a JS module. The interface is small: interface Game { public function getSlug (): string ; public function getJsModule (): string ; /** * Validate the raw client payload and compute the score server-side. * Never trust any score computed in the browser. * * @throws InvalidGamePayloadException when the payload is missing data, * malformed, or structurally impossible (manipulated). */ public function scoreResult ( array $raw ): GameScore ; } The JS module records raw events (which option, how many milliseconds) and POSTs them. One controller handles all 39 games: public function storeResult ( Request $request , string $slug ): JsonResponse { $game = $this -> registry -> get ( $slug ) ?? abort ( 404 ); $validated = $request -> validate ([ 'payload' => [ 'required' , 'array' ], 'duration_ms' => [ 'required' , 'integer' , 'min:1' , 'max:1800000' ], ]); try { $score = $game -> scoreResult ( $validated [ 'payload' ]); } catch ( InvalidGamePayloadException $e ) { return response () -> json ([ 'message' => $e -> getMessage ()], 422 ); } // store score, percentile and the raw payload… } The raw payload is stored next to the score. It costs one JSON column, and it means any later change to a scoring rule can be checked against real runs. Level 1: reject what a human can't do The cheapest check is plausibility. A reaction-time game gets five trials, and each one has to fall between 120 and 2000 ms: public const TRIALS = 5 ; public const MIN_RT_MS = 120 ; // faster than this is anticipation, not reaction public const MAX_RT_MS = 2000 ; if ( count ( $trials ) !== self :: TRIALS ) { throw new InvalidGamePayloadException ( 'A session must contain exactly 5 trials.' ); } // per trial: if ( ! is_int ( $rt ) || $rt < self :: MIN_RT_MS || $rt > self :: MAX_RT_MS ) { throw new InvalidGamePayloadException ( "Trial { $index } : 'rt_ms' outside plausible bounds." ); } The multiple-choice tests do the same with a 400 ms floor per question, and a timed test rejects a run whose answers add up to more time than the clock allows. None of this stops a determined person, but it removes the garbage: double-submits, broken clients, someone posting {"score": 100} by hand. Level 2: the answer key never reaches the browser For tests built from a fixed question bank (verbal, deductive, situational judgement), the page gets the questions and nothing else: interface ProvidesClientData { /** JSON-serialisable, with no answer key in it. */ public function clientData (): array ; } The Blade view drops that into a data attribute, and the JS reads it from there: <div id="game-root" @if ($game instanceof \App\Games\ProvidesClientData) data-game-data="{{ json_encode($game->clientData()) }}" @endif> The payload names item ids and the player's choice. The server looks the answer up itself, and it also checks that the ids make sense together: protected function isCorrect ( array $item , int $index ): bool { $statement = $item [ 'statement' ] ?? null ; $key = $this -> key (); if ( ! is_string ( $statement ) || ! isset ( $key [ $statement ])) { throw new InvalidGamePayloadException ( "Item { $index } : unknown statement." ); } if ( $key [ $statement ][ 0 ] !== ( $item [ 'passage' ] ?? null )) { throw new InvalidGamePayloadException ( "Item { $index } : the statement does not belong to that passage." ); } // …and the same statement can't be answered twice } View source on the page and you will find every question and not one answer. Level 3: seeded items the server can rebuild Some tests generate their questions procedurally. Take Aon's digit challenge: you see (_ × _) − _ = 55 and fill the blanks with digits 1–9, each once. Get one right and the next is harder; get one wrong and it gets easier. You have four minutes. If the browser generated the equations, it could also generate easy ones. If the server generated them and sent the answers along, the answers would be in the page. So the server sends a seed and the items generated from it: public function items ( int $seed ): array { $random = new Randomizer ( new Mt19937 ( $seed )); $items = []; for ( $position = 0 ; $position < self :: POSITIONS ; $position ++ ) { for ( $level = 1 ; $level <= self :: LEVELS ; $level ++ ) { $shapes = self :: SHAPES [ $level ]; $shape = $shapes [ $random -> getInt ( 0 , count ( $shapes ) - 1 )]; // Positive results only do { $digits = array_slice ( $random -> shuffleArray ( range ( 1 , 9 )), 0 , self :: slots ( $shape )); $target = self :: evaluate ( $shape , $digits ); } while ( $target < 1 ); $items [ $position ][ $level ] = [ 'shape' => $shape , 'target' => $target ]; } } return $items ; } public function clientData (): array { $seed = random_int ( 1 , 2_000_000_000 ); return [ 'seed' => $seed , 'items' => $this -> items ( $seed ), 'durationMs' => self :: DURATION_MS ]; } The page holds an item for every position and every difficulty level, because the browser doesn't know which level the player will be on. The payload returns only the seed, where the run started, and the digits typed with their timings. On submit, the server regenerates the same items from the seed and replays the adaptive staircase itself: $items = $this -> items ( $seed ); $level = 1 ; foreach ( $answers as $index => $answer ) { $item = $items [( $start + $index ) % self :: POSITIONS ][ $level ]; // validate digits and rt_ms… if ( self :: evaluate ( $item [ 'shape' ], $answer [ 'digits' ]) === $item [ 'target' ]) { $points += $level ; $level = min ( self :: LEVELS , $level + 1 ); } else { $level = max ( 1 , $level - 1 ); } } Two details worth getting right: The seeded RNG has to be explicit. PHP's Random\Randomizer with an Mt19937 engine gives the same sequence for the same seed, every time and on every machine. The global mt_rand() would have worked until some other code called it in between. The client must walk the staircase the same way the server does. The JS has its own nextLevel ( Math.min(LEVELS, Math.max(1, level + (right ? 1 : -1))) ) only to pick which item to show next. If the two ever disagreed, the player would see one equation and be scored on another, so the rule is one line on each side and nowhere else. This also checks answers the honest way: an equation can have several right fillings, and the server accepts any filling that makes it true. What this does not protect against The server doesn't remember which seeds it issued, so a player could submit a seed of their choice, or solve the page's equations offline with a script. For a free practice tool that's fine: the person cheating is the only one fooled. If this were a real assessment, I would store issued seeds with a short expiry and bind each one to the session. And a few older games still trust the client: procedural multiple-choice games where the browser builds the question and declares the right option next to the player's choice. That's a known gap, written down in the base class. Lesson two: my norms were made up, and players noticed A score only becomes useful with a percentile: "You're in the top 20%." But on day one there are no players to compare against. So I simulated them. For a timing game like Arctic Shores' Lock (press Stop while a moving shaded sector covers the highlighted digit), I modelled personal timing noise and bias, concluded that the median person is about 40 ms off target, and built the percentile table from that. At the end of each game the result screen asks, "Did you know if this score was good?" Every answer was "not really". And two new users kept landing on the 5th percentile. So I pulled the real score distributions. Nothing matched the simulations: Game Real runs What the simulated table did Lock 195 put 62% of all runs at the 5th percentile or below N-back 375 35% at the 5th percentile or below Predict 380 34% at the 5th percentile or below Numerical reasoning 137 put 55% of runs in the top 5% Flanker 614 31% in the top 5% Real Lock players have a median error of 91 ms, not 40. My best guess at what the simulation missed: people are still learning the game while they play it, and a practice run is often someone's first. The fix is boring: a percentile table is just a threshold list, so I rebuilt each one from the real distribution and wrote the source into the comment: /** * Calibrated on 195 real runs (Nov 2026): median 91 ms, p10 44 ms, p90 195 ms. * The first table came from a simulation (median person ~40 ms) * and put 62% of all runs at the 5th percentile or below. */ private const NORMS = [ 30 => 97 , 37 => 95 , 44 => 90 , 56 => 80 , 66 => 70 , 80 => 60 , 91 => 50 , // … 244 => 5 , ]; What I'd do differently: ship simulated norms labelled as provisional, log every run from day one (I did, and without it there would have been nothing to recalibrate from), and check the score distribution after the first hundred runs, not after a few hundred. Takeaways The browser reports events, the server computes the score. Keep the raw payload. Plausibility bounds remove most junk for almost no code. A question bank stays on the server; the page gets questions, never keys. Seeded generation ( Randomizer + Mt19937 ) lets the server rebuild exactly what the player saw, without storing it. Simulated norms are a placeholder. Real players will tell you how wrong they are, if you ask them on the result screen. If you want to see it in action, the games are free to play without an account: GamePrep . The digit challenge from the example above is one of them, and so is the Lock game . Questions about the scoring or the norms are welcome in the comments.

title: PostgreSQL Query Planner Internals: Statistics, Row Estimates, and the Plan Regression That Silently Kills Your p99 Latency
author: SoftwareDevs mvpfactory.io
summary: --- title : " PostgreSQL Query Planner: Fix Silent p99 Regressions" published : true description : " Stale pg_statistic data and cross-column correlations silently destroy your p99 latency. Learn how to diagnose and fix query plan regressions with extended statistics and pg_hint_plan." tags : postgresql, performance, architecture, cloud canonical_url : https://mvpfactory.co/blog/postgresql-query-planner-p99-regressions --- What You Will Learn By the end of this tutorial you will understand why your PostgreSQL queries degrade silently — no errors, no crashes, just creeping p99 spikes — and you will have three concrete fixes you can apply today. We are going deep into pg_statistic , the planner cost model, and the cross-column correlation trap that kills production systems. Prerequisites A running PostgreSQL 10+ instance Access to pg_stat_user_tables and EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) Optionally: pg_hint_plan extension installed for plan pinning How the Planner Actually Works The PostgreSQL query planner is a cost-based optimizer. It generates candidate execution plans, estimates each one's cost from a statistical model, and picks the cheapest. The critical word is estimates . Everything hinges on pg_statistic — a system catalog populated by ANALYZE that stores column-level histograms, most-common values (MCVs), and null fractions. Here is the part the docs gloss over: the planner never sees your actual data at query time. It sees a snapshot that may be hours or weeks old on a high-write table. Factor Source Risk Row count estimate pg_class.reltuples Stale after bulk inserts Selectivity per column pg_statistic MCVs + histogram Low statistics_target = coarse buckets Multi-column selectivity Assumed independent by default Correlated columns = wildly wrong estimates Join row estimates Multiplied selectivities Errors compound across joins When the planner estimates 50 rows but gets 50,000, it picks a Nested Loop over a Hash Join. Your query goes from 8ms to 4 seconds. Step 1 — Find Your Stale Tables Let me show you a pattern I use in every project. Run this first. SELECT schemaname , relname , last_analyze , last_autoanalyze , n_mod_since_analyze FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_mod_since_analyze DESC LIMIT 20 ; Any table with n_mod_since_analyze > 100k and no recent last_analyze is a plan regression waiting to happen. The autovacuum trigger is autovacuum_analyze_threshold + autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor * reltuples . On a 10M-row table with the default 0.2 scale factor, you need 2 million row changes before autovacuum analyzes. That is an enormous drift window. Step 2 — Raise statistics_target on Hot Columns The default is 100 — PostgreSQL stores 100 histogram buckets and 100 MCVs per column. For high-cardinality or skewed distributions, the planner interpolates between sparse buckets and gets selectivity estimates off by orders of magnitude. ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET STATISTICS 500 ; ANALYZE orders ; Raise this to 200–500 on any column that appears in a WHERE clause or join condition on a large table. Storage cost is negligible. Plan quality improvement on skewed distributions is not. Step 3 — Create Extended Statistics for Correlated Columns Here is the gotcha that will save you hours. The planner assumes column independence by default. If you filter on (country = 'US' AND city = 'Seattle') , it computes P(country) × P(city) . But city is highly correlated with country , so the actual selectivity is roughly just P(city) — and the planner dramatically underestimates the row count, triggering wrong join strategies. The fix, available since PostgreSQL 10: CREATE STATISTICS orders_country_city ( dependencies , ndistinct ) ON country , city FROM orders ; ANALYZE orders ; EXPLAIN ( ANALYZE , BUFFERS ) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE country = 'US' AND city = 'Seattle' ; Look for Statistics objects: orders_country_city in the EXPLAIN output. Row estimate improvement is often 10–100x on correlated columns. Common pairs to audit: (status, type) , (country, region) , (user_id, tenant_id) . Step 4 — Pin Plans in a Production Incident This is a last resort, not a first resort. But when you have a known-good plan and cannot wait for statistics to converge, pg_hint_plan lets you override the planner directly. /*+ HashJoin(o s) SeqScan(o) */ SELECT o . id , s . status FROM orders o JOIN shipments s ON s . order_id = o . id WHERE o . created_at > now () - interval '7 days' ; Document every hint you place and set a calendar reminder to remove it once statistics are properly calibrated. Hints that outlive their usefulness become the next regression. Gotchas Autovacuum is not enough on write-heavy tables. Schedule explicit ANALYZE via cron or your job queue for any table taking bulk inserts or deletes on a time-series pattern: ANALYZE VERBOSE orders , shipments , events ; Extended statistics require a follow-up ANALYZE . CREATE STATISTICS does nothing on its own — you must run ANALYZE on the table afterward or the new statistics object has no data. pg_hint_plan hints in ORM-generated queries are fragile. If your ORM rewrites the query structure, the hint may no longer match and will silently be ignored. Validate with EXPLAIN after any ORM upgrade. Conclusion The docs do not make this obvious, but every p99 regression investigation should start with pg_stat_user_tables . From there, the path is: raise statistics_target on hot columns, create extended statistics for correlated column pairs, and reach for pg_hint_plan only when the production incident demands it. These three levers have stabilized more production systems than any index change I have made. Further reading: PostgreSQL Extended Statistics pg_hint_plan documentation pg_statistic system catalog

title: Building Scalable Webhooks with Cloudflare Workers
author: Devarshi Shimpi
summary: Handling webhooks at scale presents a unique set of engineering challenges. When a third-party service (like GitHub, Stripe, or Twilio) sends an event to your application, it expects a fast, reliable, and secure response. If your server is slow, the provider might time out. If you receive a sudden spike in events, your backend could be overwhelmed. Cloudflare Workers provide a highly effective solution for this problem. By deploying serverless functions to the edge, you can intercept, validate, and queue webhooks globally with near-zero latency. In this tutorial, we will explore the best practices for building a resilient webhook architecture and introduce Codra , an open-source AI code review engine, as a reference implementation. The Challenges of Webhook Infrastructure When building a webhook receiver, developers must account for several critical factors: Latency and Timeouts: Most providers demand an HTTP 200 OK within a few seconds. If your processing takes longer, the provider will assume failure and retry. Traffic Spikes: Events often arrive in bursts. A suddenly popular repository or a large batch job can trigger thousands of webhooks concurrently. Security: Endpoints are publicly accessible. You must verify payloads to ensure they actually originated from the trusted provider. Reliability and Idempotency: Providers guarantee "at least once" delivery. Your system must handle duplicate events gracefully. Why Cloudflare Workers? Cloudflare Workers operate at the network edge, running within milliseconds of the user or provider making the request. They offer: Instant Cold Starts: Unlike traditional serverless platforms, Workers start almost instantly. Global Distribution: The webhook is received by the data center closest to the sender. Built-in Queues: Cloudflare Queues seamlessly integrate with Workers, allowing you to decouple ingestion from processing. Best Practices for Webhook Architecture To build a scalable webhook system, follow a decoupled approach. The edge worker should only validate the request and push it to a queue. 1. Verify Signatures at the Edge Never trust an incoming webhook without verifying its cryptographic signature. Providers like GitHub include a signature in the headers based on a shared secret. You can compute the HMAC signature in your Worker and compare it using a constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks. export async function verifySignature ( request , secret ) { const signature = request . headers . get ( ' x-hub-signature-256 ' ); if ( ! signature ) return false ; const body = await request . clone (). text (); const encoder = new TextEncoder (); const key = await crypto . subtle . importKey ( ' raw ' , encoder . encode ( secret ), { name : ' HMAC ' , hash : ' SHA-256 ' }, false , [ ' sign ' ] ); const signed = await crypto . subtle . sign ( ' HMAC ' , key , encoder . encode ( body )); const expectedSignature = ' sha256= ' + Array . from ( new Uint8Array ( signed )) . map ( b => b . toString ( 16 ). padStart ( 2 , ' 0 ' )) . join ( '' ); return signature === expectedSignature ; } 2. Acknowledge Fast and Queue the Work Do not process the webhook payload synchronously. Instead, push the payload to a message queue and return a 200 status code immediately. Cloudflare Queues are perfect for this. export default { async fetch ( request , env ) { if ( request . method !== ' POST ' ) { return new Response ( ' Method not allowed ' , { status : 405 }); } const isValid = await verifySignature ( request , env . WEBHOOK_SECRET ); if ( ! isValid ) { return new Response ( ' Unauthorized ' , { status : 401 }); } const payload = await request . json (); // Push to Cloudflare Queue await env . WEBHOOK_QUEUE . send ( payload ); return new Response ( ' Accepted ' , { status : 202 }); } }; 3. Handle Processing Asynchronously A separate queue consumer handles the heavy lifting. This is where you can implement retries and long-running tasks without worrying about the webhook provider timing out. export default { async queue ( batch , env ) { for ( const message of batch . messages ) { try { await processEvent ( message . body ); message . ack (); } catch ( error ) { console . error ( ' Processing failed ' , error ); message . retry (); } } } }; Reference Architecture: Introducing Codra If you are looking for a production-ready example of this architecture, check out Codra . Codra is an open-source, self-hosted AI code review engine designed specifically for GitHub pull requests. While Codra supports containerized Docker and Node.js deployments via BullMQ, its serverless deployment profile leverages Cloudflare Workers and Queues to provide an edge-native review loop with zero server maintenance ( see the Cloudflare Workers deployment guide ). Codra leverages this decoupled webhook pattern to handle pull request events efficiently. When a developer pushes code, GitHub sends a webhook to the Codra ingestion worker. The worker verifies the payload and queues the review task, ensuring GitHub never experiences a timeout. Codra focuses on providing a superior developer experience through several key features: Privacy First: It supports a "bring your own model" approach, allowing you to use your preferred LLM provider without compromising your codebase's privacy. Infrastructure Control: Whether deployed to your Cloudflare account, run via Docker on internal servers, or hosted on Node.js, your team retains complete ownership of your infrastructure, encryption keys, and review policies. Reduced Comment Noise: One of the biggest challenges with AI code reviews is spam. Codra implements multi-pass filtering to analyze the code context deeply, ensuring it only leaves high-value, actionable comments on pull requests. By examining the Codra repository or reviewing its architecture overview , developers can see how to structure large-scale Worker applications, manage secrets, and handle complex asynchronous workflows. Conclusion Building webhook infrastructure requires anticipating scale from day one. By utilizing Cloudflare Workers and Queues, developers can build a robust ingestion layer that handles traffic spikes gracefully and processes data securely. Open-source projects like Codra provide excellent blueprints for implementing these patterns in real-world scenarios.

title: Log the prompt that produced a merged UI change (tiny ADR)
author: Sherotree
summary: We merge a lot of agent UI now. Six months later someone asks “why does this form validate zip before city?” and the PR description just says “agent polish.” The diff is gone from working memory. The prompt that made the decision is gone too. I started treating the prompt that shipped like a tiny ADR. Not a ceremony. One short file (or PR note) next to the change so the next human — or the next agent — can see what we asked for , not only what landed . What goes in the tiny ADR Keep it under ~15 lines. I use this shape: ## Prompt ADR — ShippingForm zip-before-city (2026-11-05) **Goal:** Require zip before city on blur for US addresses. **Prompt (verbatim):** … **Files touched:** `ShippingForm.tsx` , `shippingValidation.ts` **Rejected alternatives:** city-first (matches old mock); shared schema with Checkout (too wide for this PR) **Follow-ups:** none / link issue Verbatim matters. Paraphrase loses the constraints the agent actually obeyed (or ignored). Why not “just read the commit”? Commits show outcome . Prompts show intent and guardrails : “Only touch ShippingForm.tsx ” explains why Checkout stayed dirty “No new deps” explains why we didn’t pull in zod “Match existing error copy keys” explains the awkward i18n string you were about to “clean up” Without that, the next agent “simplifies” the awkward bits and reopens bugs you already paid for. Where I put it Pick one place and stick to it. Mine: Preferred: docs/prompt-adrs/YYYY-MM-DD-short-slug.md in the same PR Fine: a ## Prompt used section in the PR body (copy into docs when merging) Avoid: only in chat history / only in the agent transcript Chat is not a durable design record. Repo is. Prompt I paste when starting the work You’re editing `ShippingForm` US address validation only. Before you change code, write `docs/prompt-adrs/YYYY-MM-DD-shipping-zip-before-city.md` with: - Goal (one sentence) - This prompt pasted verbatim - Files you expect to touch - Alternatives you will NOT do in this PR Then implement. Do not expand scope. If you need Checkout changes, stop and say so. Yes, I ask the agent to write the ADR first. If it skips the file, I bounce the PR before reviewing the UI. What I reject in review Reject / ask to add Agent UI PR with no prompt record and a vague “assisted by AI” checkbox ADR that says “improved UX” with no verbatim prompt Prompt buried in a screenshot of the chat Accept Short markdown in-repo Verbatim prompt + goal + files + explicit non-goals Link from PR description to the ADR path Tiny habit On the next agent UI merge, spend two minutes: paste the prompt into docs/prompt-adrs/… , list files, name one thing you didn’t do. Future you (and the next model) will treat that as source of truth instead of inventing a nicer story from the diff alone.

title: Quand ton levier cognitif le plus sous-estimé, c'est ta vision
author: Ashish
summary: Quand ton levier cognitif le plus sous-estimé, c'est ta vision Sur The Builders , Garry Tan a lâché le chiffre : 200 000 $ par an en tokens pour ses agents IA. Il dort peu, il délègue tout, il maximise son output. L'anecdote fait sourire, mais le signal est fort : les gens qui construisent l'avenir mettent gros sur leur propre levier cognitif . Et si le prochain levier, c'était ta vision ? Le point aveugle de la productivité On optimise le code, le sommeil, la nutrition, les outils. Mais la coordination binoculaire — la capacité des deux yeux à fusionner une image 3D stable — reste hors radar. Pourtant, l'amblyopie (œil paresseux) touche ~3 % des adultes, souvent non traitée après l'enfance. Fatigue visuelle, manque de profondeur, lecture lente : coûts quotidiens invisibles. Je l'ai découvert à 34 ans, un soir de décembre devant mon écran. Je terminais une PR, les yeux brûlants, et je lisais la même ligne trois fois. Pas de fatigue classique. Mon œil gauche ne « participait » plus. Le cerveau l'avait mis en standby depuis l'enfance — diagnostic à 7 ans, patch deux semaines, puis abandon. « Ça ne marche plus à ton âge », m'avait dit l'ophtalmo. Sauf que la neuroplasticité ne s'éteint pas à 18 ans. Elle demande le bon stimulus. Comment j'ai atterri sur Amblyotube Je cherchais une alternative aux exercices de brock string et aux lentilles prismatiques. Un thread HN mentionnait une app VR transformant YouTube en entraînement dichoptique. Amblyotube , de Seven Sportz pour Meta Quest (2, 3, Pro, 3S). Principe : deux flux vidéo indépendants, un par œil, pendant que tu regardes du contenu normal. Pas de routine rigide, pas de patch physique. J'ai installé l'apk depuis le Meta Quest App Store, mis le casque. Premier écran critique : choisir l'œil paresseux (gauche/droite). Message clair : « Choisir incorrectement entraîne l'œil dominant au lieu de l'œil paresseux. » J'ai sélectionné Gauche . Preset de sévérité : Modéré (ne peut pas lire les 3 à 5 dernières lignes du tableau Snellen). L'app calibre automatiquement Dominant Eye Shader et Lazy Eye Sharpener . Test LogMAR intégré : optotypes Landolt C à 3 m virtuels, algorithme en escalier, jusqu'à 30 essais par œil. Score logMAR + mise à jour automatique du profil thérapeutique. Mon résultat : 0.42 logMAR œil gauche, 0.02 œil droit. L'app a ajusté le shader. De la data, pas de devinette. Ce qui se passe vraiment dans le casque Cœur technique : MFBF ( Monocular Fixation in a Binocular Field ). L'IA détecte les silhouettes humaines dans la vidéo YouTube en temps réel et applique un sharpening sélectif sur le flux de l'œil paresseux. L'œil dominant reçoit un shader paramétrable : blur, contraste, luminosité, gamma, opacité. À 100 % d'opacité = occlusion numérique totale (patch digital). Objectif standard : transparence partielle, les deux yeux traitent l'info ensemble, le cerveau réapprend la fusion. En plus : Flicker contrôlé : « jerk » visuel sur cibles humaines forçant le cortex à prêter attention à l'œil ignoré. Magenta Focus Cue : cercle mobile magenta vif (œil paresseux) / gris subtil (dominant). Le magenta ressort sur tons peau, verts, bleus — entraîne fusion binoculaire et perception de profondeur 3D . Wedge Occlusion : coin noir sur chaque champ éliminant la rivalité binoculaire. Room View (AR) : pass-through, vidéo flottante dans ta vraie pièce. Moins d'isolement, plus de contexte proprioceptif. Visual Accents en mode MFBF : Highlight : lueur jaune-vert fluo sur personnes. Outline : contour rouge sur silhouettes. Pulse : effet « respiration » (brightness monte/descend), Pulse Hz et Pulse depth réglables. J'ai mis 1.2 Hz, depth 60 % — mon œil gauche « accrochait » les visages sans effort conscient. L'interface, côté dev Panneau de contrôle flottant en VR, redimensionnable, déplaçable. Hand tracking natif + manettes. Barre de recherche YouTube intégrée + Catalog préchargé (dessins animés, kids) utilisable offline . Lecture standard : play/pause/seek/volume/mute, sélection langue (EN/DE/FR/JA…), Reset All pour défauts du preset. J'ai lancé Kurzgesagt (ironique). 35 min plus tard, retrait du casque. Première chose : le texte sur mon 27" était plus net . Pas « moins flou » — plus net . Comme si le contraste avait été remonté côté gauche. Profondeur de champ par la fenêtre : branches d'arbre aux plans distincts. Pas un miracle. Une session. Mais mesurable . La routine qui tient 30–40 min/jour , max 1 h (consigne sécurité VR). Le matin, café à la main, avant le standup. Parfois Room View pour garder un œil sur la cuisine. Parfois salle virtuelle pour l'immersion. Ajustement hebdo : opacité shader dominant –5 %, Pulse Hz +0.1. Progression lente, intentionnelle. Test LogMAR mensuel : le mois dernier 0.38 logMAR œil gauche (gain 0.04). Pas spectaculaire. Réel . Positionnement honnête : outil d'entraînement et d'assistance visuelle supplémentaire , pas dispositif médical, ne remplace pas l'avis pro. Âge requis : 13 ans+ . Sélection œil paresseux : critique . Garde-fous dans l'app, pas cachés en petit texte. Pourquoi ça parle aux builders Garry Tan paie 200k $/an pour externaliser la cognition. Nous, on a un matériel cognitif natif — deux yeux, un cortex visuel — que la plupart sous-utilise depuis l'enfance. Coût Amblyotube : zéro (gratuit store Meta Quest). Matériel : Quest 2 d'occase ~200 €. ROI potentiel : moins de fatigue, lecture plus rapide, meilleure perception de profondeur pour 3D, CAO, review code grand écran, sim racing, ou lire la doc sans plisser les yeux. La neuroplasticité adulte existe. Elle demande répétition, signal propre, feedback. Amblyotube livre les trois dans un package qui s'intègre à une habitude existante : regarder des vidéos . Pas une nouvelle habitude. Une surcouche . Ce que j'aurais voulu savoir plus tôt Que le patch physique n'est pas la seule voie. Que l'entraînement dichoptique VR n'est pas de la SF — c'est dispo maintenant , sur hardware grand public. Que les paramètres comptent (shader, sharpening, flicker, magenta cue, wedge, accents, pulse) et sont exposés, documentés, ajustables . Que le test LogMAR intégré transforme « je crois que ça marche » en « voici le delta ». Si tu as une amblyopie résiduelle, fatigue visuelle asymétrique, ou curiosité de tester ta fusion binoculaire : essaye. Une session. Regarde les chiffres. Décide. Le levier est là. Il coûte 30 minutes par jour. https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: Box introduces feature that helps AI find relevant excerpts in documents
author: Hacks.gr
summary: Box has introduced Box Content Retrieval, integrating Nvidia's Nemotron Embed to optimize how AI assistants interact with document sets. By leveraging models that perform conceptual rather than keyword-based searches, the tool aims to improve retrieval relevance for complex tasks. Developers and enterprise users can expect the feature to roll out in early 2027, with performance targets suggesting significantly reduced token overhead and improved accuracy for large-scale data queries. Nemotron Embed prepares data in advance to aid in search. Instead of just searching for the same words, it can find related topics even when they are described in different words or in a different language. For example, according to Box, lawyers will be able to more easily find relevant clauses and legal precedents. Kari Briski, Nvidia’s vice president of productive AI software, estimates that queries will be answered four times faster, with 20% fewer errors and 90% fewer units of text processed by the AI. These numbers are Briski’s expectations. Box CEO Aaron Levie said the service can return snippets that best match the AI ​​assistant’s query or task. The service also leverages the information Box already has about documents and the controls that determine who can see them. According to Levie, this reliance on Box’s existing capabilities makes it difficult to rebuild the service from scratch. Nemotron models are available for free. ↳ READ ALSO HACKS.GR / RELATED HACKS.GR AI Unlocked Britain creates COBRA team to detect forest fires faster ↗ Box says the feature will be rolled out gradually in early 2027 to all customers with the Enterprise Advance package. author: Naraen
summary: Liquid syntax error: Tag '{%' was not properly terminated with regexp: /\%\}/
